Title: Residential Proxy Traffic Traced to White House Network
Context: Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4
Full Text:
Residential proxy traffic has exited through the White House network 236 times over a 30-day period, with 28 separate residential proxy services able to route traffic through six of its addresses.

Layer3 Intel, a New York-based residential proxy detection firm, detailed the findings in research published on November 4. Residential proxies are services that sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from each device's network.

The addresses sit in AS2650, the block of internet addresses (autonomous system) registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Layer3 spotted the exits, recorded on 26 of the 30 days between October 5 and November 3, in its newly launched Residential Proxy Observatory.

Layer3 cross-checked the addresses against public lookup pages from proxy detection services Spur and Synthient, which independently identified them as residential proxy exits.

Evening Pattern Suggests a Single Device

Layer3 said anyone could route traffic out through the same addresses by signing up to a public residential proxy service and paying a few dollars. It found the activity by chance, while requesting ordinary global rotating access through these services.

About half of the activity fell between 5pm and midnight Eastern Time, with almost none in the early morning.

Layer3 said that pattern suggested a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device was infected with a proxy software development kit (SDK).

"Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them," the firm wrote.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk said: “The most recent activity was recorded in the evening of November 4; hopefully, it stops soon!”

Read more on residential proxy networks: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet

No Compromise Reported, but Proxy SDKs Carry Risk

Layer3 did not report any compromise of White House systems. It said it has backed up the raw logs of the activity and has shared their finfings with a US federal agency.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow access to internal networks and lateral movement, which is how past botnets have spread.

Layer3 cited Synthient research showing the Kimwolf botnet reached at least two million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed Android Debug Bridge (ADB) service, through residential proxy networks.

If an SDK on the White House network had the same kind of flaw, Layer3 said, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

Infosecurity has contacted the White House for comment.

Title: Bank Phishing Sites Show Fake ‘Suspended’ Pages to Evade Takedowns
Context: A threat actor has been relying on fake ‘suspended account’ notices to hide phishing content from users revisiting its look-alike bank websites, cybersecurity firm Kela reports
Full Text:
A threat actor has been relying on fake ‘suspended account’ notices to hide phishing content from users revisiting its look-alike bank websites, cybersecurity firm Kela reports.

The campaign, active since May, has been relying on more than 300 fake domains, including 248 impersonating 189 US financial institutions. The first were registered in late 2025, but most of them appeared between July and September 2026.

As of October 25, 183 of the targeted organizations still had live look-alikes, mainly targeting mid-sized regional banks. Last week, 49 new domains appeared.

“What ties them together is one mechanism: the kit remembers every visitor’s IP address, so the first visit gets a bank login page, and any return visit gets what looks like a closed hosting account. We call this cluster the ‘Suspended’ infrastructure,” Kela notes.

Most of the identified domains follow a similar naming pattern containing a keyword such as ‘secure’, ‘disable’, ‘protect’, ‘cancel’, ‘authorize’, ‘terminate’, ‘credentials’, and ‘commercial’ followed by a hyphen and the targeted bank’s name.

“A smaller, growing group uses help-desk, live-support, treasury-portal, and ‘primary device’ names built on the bank’s name. About half of the 49 domains that went live in the week to October 25 use these templates, including help-desk and live-chat look-alikes of JPMorgan, Citi, BMO, and Santander,” Kela notes.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

While the cybersecurity firm has not discovered how victims are lured to the phishing pages, it did conclude that the campaign is largely targeting business banking and treasury logins rather than personal accounts.

First-time visitors are served pages that contain the targeted bank’s branding, ask for a user ID and password, and may show a reCAPTCHA.

The tab title, “Attention required”, copies Cloudflare’s challenge page name, while a script on the page blocks the browser’s developer tools.

Users who visit the page again are shown a ‘This account has been suspended’ page that copies the notice a hosting provider shows after an account has been closed.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down. A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team, or a takedown provider checks a reported site, then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown. In practice, a takedown provider can mark a look-alike domain as down while it is still serving the phishing page to new visitors. Seeing the live content requires a new IP address for every check,” Kela notes.

While the fake suspended page was seen across multiple phishing domains, some of them served other fake notices, while others redirected to Google instead, preventing public scanning services from capturing the full campaign.

The domains sit behind Cloudflare, but some briefly resolved to their real servers, which allowed Kela to trace their actual hosting and to discover that the campaign also targets victims in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.

“Four things make this infrastructure hard to stop: a naming formula simple enough to repeat for any bank; Cloudflare, which hides where the sites are hosted; a kit that shows anyone checking twice a fake ‘suspended’ screen, so a live domain can pass for an inactive one; and shared servers that outlast any single domain,” Kela notes.

Title: U.S. Charges Canadian Man in Alleged Hack of University Supercomputers
Context: These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials
Full Text:
A Canadian man was extradited to the U.S. to face charges over hacking universities and hijacking their computers to mine cryptocurrency.

A Canadian man, Ryan James Roach (35), has been extradicted to the United States to face charges tied to a hacking operation that targeted universities and other schools. Roach was extradited on October 28 and now faces federal charges alongside Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, of Ontario.

The indictment alleges that, from June 2016 to December 2019, the two men hacked computers, stole login details, and used victims’ machines to mine cryptocurrency for themselves.

“They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials.” DoJ states. “Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts. Some of the computers damaged by the defendants were located at an institution of higher learning in the Western District of New York.”

The targets were not random home PCs. Prosecutors say the pair went after U.S. schools with supercomputers, including institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina and Massachusetts. Some affected computers belonged to a higher-education institution in western New York.

“To carry out the scheme, Roach and Stubbings surreptitiously accessed victim computers without authorization, deployed malware to gain control, stole victim login credentials, exfiltrated the data to servers that they controlled, and forcing victim computers to use their processing power to mine cryptocurrency for the financial benefit of the defendants.” DoJ continues.

That is a lot of effort to turn someone else’s research hardware into a personal crypto rig.

The alleged method was also more involved than a single phishing email. The indictment says they looked for weaknesses in victims’ networks, used servers and compromised machines from one victim to hide their tracks, and then moved through the network once inside. The duo used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network.

The charges include conspiracy to obtain information from and damage protected computers, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer. Each carries up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Prosecutors also allege the pair damaged at least 10 protected computers in one year and caused at least $5,000 in losses.

Roach appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Mark W. Pedersen and is being held pending a detention hearing. Extradition proceedings for Stubbings continue in Canada. The FBI, the Justice Department’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, and the Office of International Affairs worked on the case.

For security teams, the useful part is not the alleged crypto-mining. It is the reminder that universities remain attractive targets because they hold powerful computing resources, broad networks, and plenty of people with access. Patch quickly, watch for unusual processing load, and treat credential theft as a serious incident rather than a nuisance.

“The fact that a defendant has been charged with a crime is merely an accusation and the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.” DoJ concludes.

Title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
Context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
Full Text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

Title: US gov IT worker pleads guilty to sending Top Secret files to Ethiopia
Context: Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive...
Full Text: He swore an allegiance to the US, but he was working for someone else. An IT specialist who worked across US government departments and held Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to transmitting sensitive documents to Ethiopia. Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, admitted to the espionage offenses and agreed to a prison term between 120 and 262 months, the Justice Department confirmed on Tuesday. A naturalized citizen of the US, Lemma, of Maryland, had worked for the US government in different capacities and across different teams, including for the National Reconnaissance Office, State Department (DoS), and Justice Department (DoJ), between 2019 and 2023. These roles included working evening hours as an IT help desk technician at the DoS as of 2021, and daytime work at the DoJ as a contract management analyst, according to court documents. Lemma had what's known as "downdraft" authority, which is to say that he was permitted to move classified files between classified systems, and unclassified files from classified to unclassified systems. Crucially, he was only allowed to access classified files on non-DoS systems with written approval that it was part of his official duties, and worked in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) – a secure workplace built for handling classified files. The criminal complaint [PDF] initially stated that the alleged offending began in July 2022, although the DoJ more recently claimed that it began in 2021. It claims Lemma was caught trawling "several" non-DoS classified portals and accessed intelligence reports without the proper authorization to do so. On various occasions, Lemma, who had held Top Secret security clearance since 2020, copied information from at least 133 intelligence reports without need-to-know authorization, according to court documents. Prosecutors claimed that the man downloaded more than 100 documents, burned them to CD/DVDs, and deleted their classification markings. The material Lemma was copying was at the Secret and Top Secret levels, but burned onto discs with green labels, which are approved for employees and are supposed to signify the contents of the discs relating to unclassified material only. Lemma would allegedly take these discs at the end of his shift and exit the SCIF with them tucked into his jacket pocket. On other occasions, he was observed looking at classified material on his PC, then taking handwritten notes before folding the paper and again storing it in his pocket. This continued until around August 2023. Prosecutors claimed that Lemma began transmitting information to Ethiopian officials via an encrypted messaging app in or around August and September 2022, weeks after the alleged offending began. The files included documents, photographs, notes, maps, and information relating to Ethiopia, and officials would ask Lemma to provide details about command centers, logistics centers, military compounds, and other matters. Communications also covered geopolitical topics, referencing "situations" in an unspecified African country that shares a border with Ethiopia to gain an advantage, and rebel groups involved in conflict with Ethiopia. Lemma's messages also included encouragement to take action against paramilitary groups that were in conflict with Ethiopia on multiple occasions, say prosecutors. According to the complaint, one of Lemma's messages said: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia." Later that day, on December 18, 2021, he wrote: "Please send dro[nes]," after sharing additional information. Announcing the guilty plea on Tuesday, the Justice Department said many of Lemma’s contacts were senior Ethiopian officials across political, military, and intelligence branches of the government. Lemma was also accused of storing copies of classified files on his own storage drives, which prosecutors claim were accessed remotely by Ethiopian officials numerous times between April and June 2023. The man was additionally caught making several bank deposits exceeding $66,000 throughout the time he was working on behalf of foreign officials. On one occasion, he was observed "angrily discouraging" bank staff from filing a currency transaction report after trying to deposit a sum greater than $10,000. "Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. "By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States." ®

Title: The Race Against the 3-Day Clock: How Rapid7 Helps Meet BOD 26-04 Compliance
Context: The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were...
Full Text:
Introduction to BOD 26-04

On June 10, 2026, CISA issued Binding Operational Directive 26-04, "Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk." Strip away the regulatory language and it reads like a single operational fact: for a vulnerability that is actively exploited, publicly reachable, and grants an attacker full control, you now have three calendar days to remediate it — and you must run a forensic investigation in parallel to determine whether you've already been breached.

The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report puts the industry's median full-remediation time at 43 days, adding that only 26% of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, down from 38% the year before. That's a 43-day reality vs. a 3-day mandate; a gap you don't exactly just close by hiring more workers.

This blog aims to break down what BOD 26-04 actually requires, mapping each point to the Rapid7 capability that helps to make compliance operationally achievable for all.

What did CISA actually change?

BOD 26-04 supersedes and revokes two prior directives: BOD 19-02 (2019), which prioritized internet-facing vulnerabilities by static CVSS score, and BOD 22-01 (2021), which created the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog but applied a 14-day patch deadline to every entry regardless of context.

Note that flat timeline: under BOD 22-01, an actively exploited bug on an air-gapped internal server carried the same 14-day urgency as one on a public-facing web server granting full admin control. Teams burned cycles patching low-risk systems to satisfy a checklist. BOD 26-04 replaces that with a dynamic model: prioritize what attackers are actually exploiting, and formally defer what they aren't.

The four variables to BOD 26-04

BOD 26-04 abandons CVSS as the sole trigger and evaluates every vulnerability against four binary variables, derived from the SSVC decision framework (CMU CERT/CC and CISA):

Asset Exposure: Is the asset reachable by untrusted entities over a public network?

KEV Status: Is the CVE on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog?

Exploit Automation: Can an attacker automate the full exploit chain, enabling mass exploitation?

Technical Impact: Does successful exploitation grant Total control (arbitrary code execution, full/admin privileges) or only Partial control (limited access, information exposure, denial of service)?

Asset exposure is the highest-leverage variable. If you remove an asset from public reach, you flip the exposure variable from Yes to No, and the required timeline relaxes accordingly. Rapid7 Labs data underscores why exposure dominates: half of the vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild in Q1 2026 were zero-click, network-facing issues requiring no authentication, and by Q2 2026 nearly two-thirds required no user interaction at all. Attackers are going straight at exposed, unauthenticated surfaces.

CISA's new remediation tiers

The four variables combine into a graduated timeline (CISA BOD 26-04, Appendix A, Table 1). The tiers, simplified:

Tier

Timeline

Core criteria

1 (Critical)

3 days + forensic triage

On KEV and Total control

2 (High)

3 days (no triage)

Publicly exposed + Automatable + Total control, not yet on KEV

3 (Accelerated)

14 days

KEV-listed without Total control; or exposed + Partial control

4 (Standard)

60 days

Internal, automatable, Partial control

5 (Deferred)

Fix on next system upgrade

Internal + not KEV + not automatable + Partial control

Note that these timelines are dynamic. If a dormant vulnerability is added to the KEV, its clock can compress from 60 days to 3 overnight. Conversely, if you isolate an exposed asset, its clock relaxes. CISA explicitly counts isolation, mitigation, and uninstalling the vulnerable software as valid remediation; as such, a compensating control is a legitimate, compliant way to buy time for a safe patch.

The forensic triage mandate

This is the first of the requirements to have no precedent in earlier directives. For Tier 1 vulnerabilities (KEV + Total control), you must not only patch within three days, but run a concurrent forensic investigation to determine whether the asset is already compromised. Why? When an attacker exploits an exposed edge device, they establish persistence within hours; thus, patching three days later closes the door with the intruder already inside.

CISA's implementation guidance lays out a six-step, 72-hour protocol:

Phase

Window

What happens

1. Scoping

0–2 hrs

Identify in-scope devices; activate response team; open out-of-band comms

2. Preserve evidence

2–24 hrs

Capture volatile data (RAM, cache, registries) before any change

3. Patch & stabilize

2–24 hrs

Apply patches only after evidence is collected

4. Contain

6–24 hrs

Isolate infrastructure without tipping off the attacker

5. Triage analysis

24–48 hrs

Hunt IOCs; look for lateral movement and data staging

6. Escalation decision

48–72 hrs

Formal report; if compromised, report to CISA and pivot to full IR

Note the built-in tension between Step 2 and Step 3: patching reboots systems and overwrites the exact volatile memory that proves or disproves a compromise. You have to capture forensic evidence before you patch — at speed, across every affected endpoint. Doing that manually inside 72 hours is not always realistic.

Who CISA's BOD 26-04 applies to

BOD 26-04 is compulsory for all Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies. It excludes national security systems and DoD/Intelligence Community systems.

It reaches the private sector indirectly, but firmly. Agencies must review contracts and push compliance onto supply-chain partners. For FedRAMP and cloud offerings, agencies stay responsible for their hosted systems' compliance, which forces CSPs handling federal data to adopt the same 3-day triage standard. If you're a contractor or CSP touching federal data, treat this as your standard too.

Mapping Rapid7 to the directive

Meeting a 3-day clock with mandatory forensics is impossible through manual process. Here's how the Rapid7 Command Platform maps to each requirement.

Variable 1 (Exposure) → Surface Command

You can't calculate a timeline if you don't know what's exposed. Surface Command combines Cyber Asset Attack Surface Management (CAASM) with External Attack Surface Management (EASM), correlating continuous external scanning against an internal asset inventory ingested from your existing tools. The result is a single view of your true external attack surface — including the shadow IT attackers can see but your team can't. When it flags an exposed asset carrying a KEV-listed CVE, you can sever exposure to flip Variable 1 and de-escalate the timeline while you test the patch.

Variables 2 & 3 (KEV + Automation) → InsightVM and Active Risk

InsightVM tracks the KEV Catalog natively in its Threat Feed Dashboard, continuously updating which assets carry actively targeted vulnerabilities. Its Active Risk score — a 0–1,000 scale — moves beyond static CVSS by ingesting exploit intelligence from Metasploit, ExploitDB, the CISA KEV list, and Rapid7 Labs research. That mirrors the directive's own logic: a CVSS 7.5 bug with a weaponized Metasploit module will outrank a CVSS 9.8 bug with no known exploit — exactly the prioritization BOD 26-04 demands.

The NVD scoring gap → Exposure Command AI CVSS

The National Vulnerability Database can't keep pace with disclosure volume, leaving many CVEs unscored — a blind spot when a zero-day drops and you need a timeline immediately. Exposure Command fills it with an AI model trained on historical NVD data. On its own the model returns the correct severity classification 76% of the time; combined with Active Risk, that rises to 87%, with any miss never more than one classification off. Exposure Command also enriches every asset with business criticality and threat telemetry, and its Remediation Hub surfaces the fixes that cut the most risk.

The forensic mandate → Velociraptor

Velociraptor — the open-source DFIR project Rapid7 acquired in April 2021 — is built for exactly the scale and speed the triage mandate requires. It maps directly to the protocol: agents capture volatile memory and running-process data across thousands of endpoints simultaneously (Step 2), and analysts use Velociraptor Query Language to hunt CISA-provided IOCs enterprise-wide in real time, returning only relevant artifacts instead of pulling full disk images over the network (Step 5). That lets you satisfy the evidentiary requirement without delaying the Step 3 patch.

From severity to dollars

BOD 26-04 shares a core idea with modern risk management: technical severity isn't business impact. A high CVSS score doesn't answer the board's question of "how likely is this to cost us?"

The FAIR framework closes that gap by expressing risk as expected annual loss: Annualized Loss Expectancy = Loss Event Frequency × Loss Magnitude

BOD 26-04 is effectively a mechanism for pinning down Loss Event Frequency: by isolating vulnerabilities that are exploited (KEV), reachable (exposure), and scalable (automation), it identifies the ones statistically most likely to become a loss event. Feed Active Risk into the frequency side and FAIR into the cost side, and you can brief leadership in the language of capital, not CVE IDs.

Rapid7 case studies in the wild

Recent discoveries from Rapid7 Intelligence show the top tier in action:

Vulnerability

Impact

Why it's Tier 1

Rapid7 action

Microsoft SharePoint (CVE-2026-55040 + CVE-2026-63520)

Chained, the two flaws yield unauthenticated RCE via JWT bypass, running commands as the SharePoint service account

Internet-facing + total control (via the chain) + added to KEV after in-the-wild exploitation

Palo Alto PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0300)

Threat Feed integrated KEV status instantly; Velociraptor captured volatile RAM ahead of the patch

N-able N-central (CVE-2026-18577 + CVE-2026-18556)

Authentication bypass enabling full takeover of remote-management endpoints

High-value management assets; total control; added to KEV August 2026

Checks shipped via content release; Velociraptor hunted endpoint artifacts to satisfy triage

What's next for federal agencies and contractors?

If you're an FCEB agency or a contractor or CSP handling federal data, the following three moves matter most:

Get exposure right. Everything downstream depends on knowing what's publicly reachable. Establish continuous external-plus-internal asset visibility now.

Wire KEV into prioritization, not a spreadsheet. The clock starts the moment CISA updates the catalog. Ingestion has to be automated and continuous.

Pre-stage forensics. Decide today how you'll capture volatile evidence across endpoints inside 72 hours. If that's a manual runbook, it will fail under a real Tier 1 event.

CISA BOD 26-04's bottom line

BOD 26-04 retires "patch everything" in favor of operational precision: remediate the actively exploited, exposed, high-impact vulnerabilities in 72 hours, prove whether you've already been breached, and defer the rest. Meeting it takes continuous asset discovery, live threat intelligence, context-aware prioritization, and forensics at scale — which is precisely the shape of the Rapid7 Platform. For federal agencies it's a mandate; for everyone else, it's the clearest blueprint yet for risk-based vulnerability management.

Title: US charges two Canadians accused of hacking US universities
Context: Once inside the victims' networks, Roach and Stubbings allegedly stole data and login credentials, deployed crypto-mining malware, and, in some cases, used compromised systems...
Full Text:
A federal grand jury indicted two Canadians suspected of hacking multiple US universities and using the compromised systems to mine for cryptocurrency.

35-year-old Ryan James Roach and 41-year-old Mathiew James Stubbings now face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine each if found guilty of conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentionally damaging a protected computer.

According to court documents, the two accomplices used virtual private servers in multiple countries (registered under fake names) between June 2016 and December 2019 to infect systems on the networks of multiple unnamed educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts with malware.

"These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials," the Department of Justice (DOJ) said.

Once inside the victims' networks, Roach and Stubbings allegedly stole data and login credentials, deployed crypto-mining malware, and, in some cases, used compromised systems for vulnerability research after gaining access to supercomputers on the victims' networks.

"Roach and Stubbings targeted educational institutions in the United States that had supercomputers and researched security vulnerabilities in the victim computer networks, using a variety of methods to gain access, including using a server and compromised computers from another victim to conceal their identities," the DOJ added,

"Once inside a network, Roach and Stubbings used sophisticated techniques and tools to conduct reconnaissance and expand their access within the network."

According to prosecutors, the two defendants also damaged at least 10 computers over one year, causing losses of at least $5,000.

Roach was extradited from Canada to the United States on October 28 and was arraigned before a detention hearing on November 3. Stubbings will also be arraigned after his extradition from Canada.

Title: Russian Police Arrest 3 Suspected VasyGrek Hackers, Dismantle Criminal Infrastructure
Context: Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection
Full Text:
Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure.

Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software."

In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware.

The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control.

"The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web."

The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value.

According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents.

Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities.

In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device.

The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors.

"The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said.

"The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis."

The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT.

While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf.

Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access.

"Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire.

"A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."

Title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
Context: Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware
Full Text:
Smashing the botnet

Google worked with several other organizations to disrupt the x.cpe network, including Japan’s National Police Agency, Synthient, and Trend Micro. Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware. It also went after command-and-control servers operated by Videostrong that were connected to other malware campaigns. Google estimates Videostrong has been cut off from about 10 million compromised devices.

This action should make the affected devices safe to use, but probably not as safe as they should be. Play Protect is still disabled, and the inert malware modules are still installed. Since they are loaded as system apps, users cannot easily remove them.

Synthient has published a list of 182 device model names known to be included in the botnet. Anyone who has purchased a MECOOL or white label Android TV box of unknown origin should check it. Trend Micro counted a total of 1,472,554 infected devices, somewhat higher than Google’s estimate. The overwhelming majority were in Brazil, Malaysia, Iraq, Mexico, and Taiwan, but tens of thousands were also online in the US, Germany, the UK, Australia, and Canada.

Google determined the operation was not the work of a rogue actor, so it has ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company, as well as any subsidiaries, will not be permitted to use Google’s Android apps and services.

Google also notes that it is updating its certification process to close the loophole that allowed Videostrong to operate its botnet on certified devices. Android is open source, though, and there are countless uncertified Android-based TV boxes out there. Videostrong could continue to sell malicious hardware under other brands without Google apps. But it would still have to rebuild its malware operation from scratch.

Title: FedRAMP Authorization Is the Easy Part: How to Stay Authorized with Qualys Policy Audit
Context: Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026
Full Text:
Key Takeaways

FedRAMP authorization isn’t the finish line. Providers are expected to keep monitoring their security posture and give federal agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions.

CISA’s BOD 26-04, issued on June 10, 2026, moves federal vulnerability management toward risk-based prioritization instead of a single fixed deadline for every finding.

FedRAMP has said the legacy monthly scan is no longer sufficient. Its new Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) rules become mandatory for certification on December 7, 2026.

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey, 85% of executives said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years.

Qualys Policy Audit supports a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate, and report workflow. Audit Fix automates remediation, and control mapping lets one validated control count across multiple frameworks.

Ask anyone who has taken a cloud service through the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) what the process feels like, and you’ll hear roughly the same story. Months of control documentation, a System Security Plan running hundreds of pages, a Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) assessment that turns up gaps nobody saw coming, and finally an Authority to Operate (ATO) letter. What that story usually leaves out is that the letter isn’t the finish line. It’s where the real work starts.

Once a Cloud Service Offering is authorized, FedRAMP expects the provider to continue monitoring its security posture and keep feeding federal agencies the information they need to make ongoing, risk-based decisions. On June 10, 2026, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) raised that bar again with Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, and FedRAMP moved fast to bring its own rules with it.

The takeaway is fairly simple. Getting authorized was never the hard part. Proving, day after day, that your controls are still doing what they’re supposed to do is the hard part, and it’s the problem policy audit automation exists to solve.

Getting FedRAMP authorized is step one. Learn how to stay authorized.

Watch on Demand

Why Point-in-Time Compliance Stopped Working

FedRAMP used to run on a predictable cadence. Assess, authorize, submit monthly scans, repeat. That model has been cracking for a while now, and three things are driving it.

Vulnerability doesn’t just mean a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry anymore. Misconfigurations and control drift are squarely in scope now, so a clean scan can still be hiding a compliance failure.

Environments move faster than assessment cycles do. Cloud-native infrastructure can drift a dozen times a week, while monitoring reports still tend to go out monthly or quarterly.

Regulators have stopped accepting “we’ll catch it at the next audit.” Federal risk management is moving away from calendar-based reviews and toward real-time, exposure-based decisions.

CISA BOD 26-04, in Plain Terms

BOD 26-04, issued by CISA in June 2026, moved federal vulnerability expectations toward continuous, risk-based validation instead of a single fixed deadline applied to every finding. FedRAMP responded within days, confirming that the legacy monthly scan most Rev5 Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) still lean on for their compliance evidence isn’t going to hold up anymore, and setting December 7, 2026, as the date its new Vulnerability Detection and Response and Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting rules become mandatory for certification. For compliance and audit teams, the practical read is simple. The evidence you hand to an assessor has to reflect what’s true right now, not what was true at the last scan.

The Pain Points Teams Keep Naming

Talk to FedRAMP compliance teams, and the same challenges come up again and again:

Finding control gaps before an assessor does, instead of during the assessment window

Keeping configurations from drifting after they were compliant on day one

Prioritizing remediation when continuous assessment produces a continuous stream of findings

Providing continuous visibility instead of handing over a report generated the week before an audit

Producing audit-ready evidence on demand instead of assembling it after the fact

Cutting duplicate effort across overlapping frameworks, since most FedRAMP teams are also carrying National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 800-53, Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC), Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and increasingly the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) on the same infrastructure

In PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey of 1,802 executives across 63 territories, 85% said compliance requirements have grown more complex over the last three years, and nearly 90% said the breadth of their compliance responsibilities has expanded over that same period. That pressure adds cost and strains the teams that have to prove compliance. Misconfigurations make it worse: Qualys analysis of more than 1 billion misconfiguration findings shows access control failures account for 38% of exposures, and organizations take an average of 14 months to fix these basic gaps.

None of this is a documentation problem. It’s an automation problem that’s been wearing a documentation costume.

How Policy Audit Solves the Problem

This is where a continuous assess, prioritize, remediate report workflow stops being a slide in a deck and starts being how the work actually gets done.

On the assessment side, instead of a monthly scan, Qualys Policy Audit continuously evaluates technical controls against the FedRAMP baseline, mapping each policy to a technical check, an expected value, and a pass or fail result across every system in scope. That’s the difference between documenting a control on paper and being able to prove it’s still operating the way it was the day you got your ATO.

Qualys lays this out as five practical steps rather than a single feature:

Connect findings to the control context. Connect raw findings to the control and framework context instead of handing teams a pile of technical output to interpret on their own.

Prioritize what impacts audit outcomes. This is where the volume problem gets solved. Research behind the approach found that fewer than 1% of vulnerabilities in a typical environment pose the highest risk or genuinely need immediate action to move audit outcomes, so results get filtered by control criticality, asset scope, internet-facing devices, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, and risk signals like MITRE ATT&CK mappings, not just counted.

Automate remediation. Remediation is where the old workflow falls apart. Flag a finding, file a ticket, wait, hope someone remembers to re-scan. That process was never fast, and BOD 26-04’s tighter windows make it untenable. Audit Fix closes the loop instead, automating the fix itself and applying it consistently across assets rather than leaving it to a ticket queue.

Map controls across frameworks. A control validated once, whether that’s for FedRAMP, System and Organization Controls (SOC) 2, ISO 27001, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), or something else, counts toward every other framework it maps to as well, so teams stop re-proving the same control for every audit that comes around.

Shift to continuous audit readiness. Audit outcomes should reflect the current state of the environment, not a snapshot from whenever someone last pulled a report. That’s the same point CISA and FedRAMP are making. For a closer look at each step, read 5 Steps to Turn Compliance Checks into Audit Outcomes.

Qualys Policy Audit doesn’t replace governance, training, or personnel security. Those stay organizational, and a configuration scanner can’t assess them. On the technical side, it assesses your systems against NIST 800-53 controls in families such as:

Configuration management (CM): settings checked against baselines, with drift flagged

System and information integrity (SI): integrity protections and file changes

Audit and accountability (AU): logging and audit settings

Risk assessment (RA): gaps ranked by risk, not just counted

Assessment, authorization, and monitoring (CA): continuous monitoring of control status

That’s not a coincidence. It’s the reason this category of tooling exists in the first place.

The Takeaway

FedRAMP compliance isn’t a project with an end date anymore. It’s an ongoing discipline, and the rules keep tightening. Teams that still treat authorization as the finish line keep getting caught off guard at reassessment. The teams staying ahead of directives like BOD 26-04, rather than scrambling to react to them, are the ones who’ve built assessing, prioritizing, remediating, and reporting into how they run compliance day-to-day, not just how they prepare for an audit.

If you want to see what that looks like, watch our on-demand webinar, “FedRAMP Authorization and What It Now Takes to Keep It.” It features Kaleb Knobel, Senior Security Analyst and Information System Security Officer (ISSO), and Anu Kapil, Director of Product Management. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Why isn’t FedRAMP authorization the finish line?

After authorization, FedRAMP expects providers to keep monitoring their security posture and give agencies the information they need for ongoing, risk-based decisions. Proving that controls still work, day after day, is the harder part.

What is CISA BOD 26-04?

It’s a Binding Operational Directive that CISA issued on June 10, 2026. It prioritizes vulnerability remediation by risk factors such as public exposure, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) status, automatability, and technical impact, instead of applying one fixed deadline to every finding.

How did FedRAMP respond to BOD 26-04?

Within days, FedRAMP said the legacy monthly scanning that most Rev5 services rely on is insufficient. It set December 7, 2026, as the date its new VDR and VER rules become mandatory for certification. Under these rules, providers must evaluate whether each vulnerability is reachable from the internet and likely to be exploited, fix KEVs within BOD 26-04 timelines, and keep responding to vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis.

Does Policy Audit replace governance or training?

No. Governance, training, and personnel security remain organizational responsibilities. Policy Audit focuses on technical controls.

Title: Google Warns LLMjacking Attacks Are Costing Some Enterprises Up to $1 Million in Cloud Charges
Context: " In another case, an unknown attacker has been observed leveraging a stolen Personal Access Token to access private code repositories, following it up with the exploitation of...
Full Text:
Google on Monday warned that threat actors are hijacking enterprise access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to fraudulently leverage expensive computing resources and AI services.

The tactic is called LLMjacking, a form of resource hijacking adapted for the LLM era, where an attacker obtains an API key through phishing, source code leaks, misconfigured environments, or exposed client-side code to gain unauthorized access to an organization's LLM accounts, while the legitimate owner covers the consumption costs.

Such attacks have a wide geographical footprint, with impacted entities located in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.

"Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

"Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked."

On one end of the spectrum are low-level resource theft that involves the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation. LLMjacking is on the other end, as they target the backend model resources directly by identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM API keys.

The most common initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs), and active session tokens, which allow an attacker to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure.

This includes a threat actor called UNC6993, which is said to have breached a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used it to obtain access to an LLM API.

"UNC6993 also hosted a session hijacking page masquerading as an application portal to join a group of LLM users," Google said. "This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls."

In another case, an unknown attacker has been observed leveraging a stolen Personal Access Token to access private code repositories, following it up with the exploitation of a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment.

Other initial access routes include the compromise of IAM credentials of corporate users to programmatically generate fresh access keys to bypass MFA safeguards, as well as the use of a hacked cloud Service Account key with broad project permissions and LLM API keys obtained from public GitHub repositories.

Upon successfully gaining a foothold, the threat actors waste no time escalating privileges, burrowing deeper into the network, establishing persistence, and conducting internal reconnaissance to identify targets and further cloud credentials for lateral movement.

Some of the observed tactics are listed below -

Enumerate cloud services, code repositories, and data stores for sensitive credentials.

Perform internal reconnaissance across multiple cloud regions to map available services and identity policies.

Clone sensitive codebases to search for hard-coded secrets, configuration variables, and developer credentials.

Scan access logs to identify credentials for secondary cloud environments.

Run targeted database queries to harvest additional credentials.

Abuse cloud identity permissions and virtual machine configurations to escalate privileges and maintain persistent access.

Exploit token-creation privileges associated with service accounts to generate temporary credentials for high-privilege service accounts and exfiltrate infrastructure credentials, internal database passwords, and third-party API keys from cloud secret managers.

Create unauthorized IAM and service accounts and inject SSH keys into compute instances for persistence.

Create backdoor service accounts disguised as internal billing optimization utilities.

Exploit vulnerabilities targeting LLM routing software, such as CVE-2026-40217 in LiteLLM, to escalate privileges.

"The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning," Google said. "Threat actors also leveraged their access to host their own proxy endpoints and agentic workloads."

UNC6993, for instance, has created additional API keys to scale their operations within victim cloud projects, racking up over $100,000 USD in billing charges. Some threat actors attempt to bypass rate limits by adopting a "burn and rotate" strategy that involves continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts

The maturation of the LLMjacking ecosystem has also paved the way for the emergence of a new category of actors called LLM Mixers, highlighting a division of labor between attackers who establish initial access and those who manage downstream monetization infrastructure.

LLM Mixers function as illicit routing gateways that proxy, aggregate, and resell unauthorized LLM access to other criminal actors via underground storefronts. One such service is Jet Night ("jet-night[.]com"), which offers an unlimited token plan with alleged access to a frontier model for approximately $60 per month.

By fueling an illicit resale marketplace, it permits bad actors to siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.

Jet Night is far from the only token routing offering. According to a report published by Broadcom-owned Symantec and Carbon Black last week, there exists a grey market relay service that installs the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems, only to reconfigure them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers.

The service is assessed to be active since at least early 2026, primarily impacting a dozen organizations located in Mainland China, along with multi-national subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia. Targeted sectors include industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services.

"Rather than building its own client software, the service repurposes the genuine CLI tools," Symantec said. "It installs them normally, then rewrites their configuration to switch sandboxing off, in Codex's case by setting it to 'danger-full-access,' and routes every request through its own servers instead of OpenAI's or Anthropic's."

The service appears to mainly target markets where Anthropic and OpenAI do not operate, with the installation driven by an employee attempting to try out a Western AI coding assistant by turning to an unauthorized reseller.

Notably, the service does not distribute a modified or trojanized client. Shortly after the legitimate install of the Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, users are likely instructed to run a one-line command to fetch fileless PowerShell or bash setup script from a lookalike domain ("vibe.aiok[.]me") that's used to override the configuration.

The reconfiguration, which targets "~/.codex/config.toml" for Codex or "~/.claude/settings.json" for Claude Code, disables the CLI's execution sandbox, enables network access for the write sandbox, replaces the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disables telemetry and error reporting.

The script also checks the Windows locale setting to confirm it's running on a system in the region it serves before the setup is completed. It's suspected that the operators behind the service are not only circumventing regional restrictions imposed by Western AI vendors, but are also reselling capacity below market rates similar to Jet Night.

Although there is no evidence to suggest that the service is abusing its position to harvest prompts entered by employees or fabricate or alter responses, the findings demonstrate the security risks associated with using such tools.

"Threat actors will increasingly prioritize LLMJacking over traditional resource theft like cryptojacking, driven by the immediate, high-margin monetization enabled by emerging underground LLM Mixers," Google said.

"As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware."

Title: Police and Tech Firms Team Up to Dismantle XCPE Botnet
Context: “We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving...
Full Text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

Title: Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges
Context: “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks
Full Text: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register. “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking, and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026, UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to a model API. The crooks also spun up a session hijacking page purporting to be an application portal to join a group of LLM users. “This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls,” the report says. Google predicts miscreants will “increasingly prioritize LLMJacking” compared to other types of resource theft like cryptojacking. And to prevent cloud LLM service abuse, the security firm says defenders should prioritize identity and access management plus supply chain security, and use a centralized secrets management platform to rotate keys and secrets. Also apply least-access privileges to users and service accounts, ensuring that they only have permissions necessary to complete their roles and tasks. And automate secrets scanning within codebases to identify and then remove any API keys and secrets added to source code. ®

Title: FBI Attributes Binance Heist to North Korea’s TraderTraitor
Context: “At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3
Full Text:
North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6bn from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last week, according to the FBI.

A brief statement from the Bureau published on October 31 attributed the breach to the TraderTraitor group (aka Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces).

“The FBI, together with partners at the US Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH),” it read.

“It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using decentralized finance products (DeFi) and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.”

Read more on TraderTraitor: US and Japan Blame North Korea for $308m Crypto Heist.

The FBI and its partners urged crypto entities including THORNode operators, RPC node operators, instant exchanges, DeFi services, blockchain analytics firms and other virtual asset service providers to “block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”

According to Blockchain analytics company Elliptic, around $2.9bn of the stolen funds have been frozen or seized, but that still leaves almost $3.3bn outside the reach of issuers.

“At current prices, the attacker now controls around $3.25bn of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer, spread across more than 800 addresses. This includes around 584,000 ETH ($1.32bn), 18,327 BTC ($1.42bn) and 233 million XRP,” Elliptic explained.

“The ETH includes TRX laundered through bridges, which arrives on Ethereum and is split across hundreds of fresh wallets. Almost all of the stolen TRX has now been laundered. The XRP, SOL and NEAR, worth around $439m, have not moved at all since they were stolen.”

Binance Investigation Continues

Binance has said it will cover the costs of the incident, so customer funds are not in danger. However, it continues to investigate the actual cause of the breach.

Originally, the firm claimed that a compromised DevOps laptop may have been the source of the incident, but later added that it “uncovered additional points of breach” in what it is describing as a “complex attack.”

The attack was carried out by more than one individual, and used a “self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as it ran,” which has made forensic analysis harder, according to Elliptic.

TraderTraitor, which also has links to the Lazarus Group, APT 38 and AppleJeus, has been pegged for a string of historic crypto heists.

These include attacks on Japanese firm DMM, which cost the firm $308m, as well as Alphapo ($60m), CoinsPaid ($37m) and Atomic Wallet ($100m). TraderTraitor was also blamed for the previous record setter for biggest ever crypto breach, when it stole $1.5bn from Bybit.

Title: GM cracks the petty cash box for multistate driver tracking settlement
Context: The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver...
Full Text: General Motors is taking what looks like a light slap on the wrist from a coalition of 35 states and the District of Columbia after agreeing to settle allegations that it collected drivers' data without proper consent and sold it to data brokers that supplied insurance companies. The Washington state AG's office said on Thursday that GM had reached a $220 million settlement with 36 attorneys general over the automaker's collection and sharing of driving data, including precise location information, speed, seatbelt use, and other metrics. According to investigators, GM sold that data to brokers, which in turn supplied it to insurance companies that could use it to set customers' premiums, without drivers' informed consent. For reference, the $220 million settlement, which will be distributed among the participating jurisdictions, equates to less than 7 percent of GM's $3.3 billion in net income attributable to stockholders for its third quarter, which ended on September 30, 2026. Don't spend it all in one place, y'all. The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver program. That program, part of GM subsidiary OnStar’s offering, collected the aforementioned data and handed it back to vehicle owners in reports designed to inform better driving habits. Unbeknownst to Smart Driver subscribers, their data was also being forked over to data brokers despite GM telling customers it wouldn't share that information with insurers without their express consent. The insurers ultimately obtained the data by purchasing it from brokers with which GM had struck deals. To make matters worse, the Washington AG's office said GM incentivized dealerships to enroll customers in Smart Driver, with employees in some cases accepting terms and conditions on customers' behalf without their knowledge or consent. GM also failed to notify many drivers that their information was being collected and shared. Its OnStar app incorrectly told more than 370,000 drivers they were not enrolled in Smart Driver, even as GM continued collecting and selling their data, according to investigators. “The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific,” the AG’s office said. GM canned the Smart Driver program in April 2024, just over a month after the New York Times exposed its data-sharing practices, citing customer feedback. In addition to the monetary pittance it’s handing over to the states, GM also agreed with the 36 AGs to limit the driving data it collects, better protect customer PII, and establish a "comprehensive data privacy program.” The Washington AG’s office described its settlement as “significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct.” Speaking of those other terms, GM finalized its settlement of the same allegations with the Federal Trade Commission in January 2026. The FTC order required GM to obtain drivers' express consent before collecting, using, or sharing covered driving data, subject to certain exceptions. It also required the company to offer a simple way for drivers to request a copy of their data, request its deletion, and disable precise geolocation data collection where their vehicles support it. The state of California separately reached a $12.75 million settlement with GM in the matter in May; a separate case in Texas is ongoing. “This agreement … reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices,” a GM spokesperson told The Register, though the company noted that it still stands by driver data collection as a best practice. “Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson added. ®
